client: I've been really struggling since my partner moved abroad for work about six months ago. At first I thought I could handle the distance, but lately I just feel this constant loneliness, like there's this hollow feeling that doesn't go away even when we video call. I'm not sure talking about it is actually going to change anything, since the situation itself isn't going to change anytime soon.
therapist:
It makes complete sense that you're feeling that hollowness — long-distance relationships ask so much of us emotionally, and six months of carrying that weight is genuinely hard. I also hear your skepticism about talking, and I want to honor that; while we can't change the distance itself, we can explore what's happening in your thoughts and daily life that might be making the loneliness feel even heavier than it has to. 

I'm curious — when that hollow feeling shows up most strongly, what kinds of thoughts tend to be running through your mind in those moments?

client: Honestly, when it hits hardest — usually at night after we hang up the phone — I just keep thinking that he's out there living his life and I'm here, kind of... frozen in place waiting for him. Like I start wondering if I even cross his mind as much as he crosses mine, and then I feel guilty for doubting him because he hasn't actually done anything wrong. It's this loop that just goes around and around and I can't seem to get off it.
therapist:
That loop you're describing — doubt, then guilt for doubting — is so exhausting, and it makes sense your mind goes there in those quiet moments after you hang up, when the contrast between connection and separation feels sharpest. What I notice is that the thought "I'm frozen while he's living his life" might be worth gently examining, because it sounds like it's framing things in a way that's quite painful for you. 

When you imagine what your days actually look like compared to six months ago, do you think that "frozen" picture really captures the full truth of how you've been living?

client: I mean... I guess if I'm being honest, I have done some things. I started that online course, I've been showing up to work even when it's hard. But it still feels like those things don't really count, like they're just me treading water while he's out there actually building something new and exciting with his life. The "frozen" feeling is so strong that it kind of drowns out everything else, even when I try to remind myself of what I have done.
therapist:
What you just did there is really significant — you found real evidence that contradicts the "frozen" story, and yet your mind quickly moved to discount it as "just treading water," which tells us something important about how this thought pattern protects itself. Starting a course and showing up consistently through pain aren't small things; they're actually acts of quiet courage, even if they don't feel dramatic or exciting from the inside. 

I'm wondering — if your partner described those same actions to you about *himself*, would you also dismiss them as not counting, or would you see them differently?

client: Honestly, if he told me he'd been showing up to something consistently while dealing with pain, I'd probably tell him that was really impressive. But it feels different when it's me — like I'm too close to it to give myself the same credit. I don't know why I can see it clearly for someone else but it just... doesn't land the same way when I try to apply it to myself.
therapist:
You've just noticed something really profound about yourself — that you have a generous, clear-eyed perspective available to you, but there's something that blocks it from turning inward, and simply naming that gap is actually the first step toward bridging it. This double standard we hold for ourselves versus others is incredibly common, but that doesn't make it fair to you, and it's something we can gently work with over time. 

I'm curious — when you imagine offering yourself even just a fraction of the compassion you'd give your partner in the same situation, what comes up for you... does it feel possible, or does something inside resist it?

client: When I try to imagine being kind to myself the way I would be to my partner... honestly, something in me kind of recoils from it. Like there's a voice that says I don't deserve that same softness, that my situation is different somehow, that I actually should have known better. It feels almost self-indulgent to let myself off the hook, even though I know logically that's not what compassion really means.
therapist:
That voice telling you that you "should have known better" is worth paying attention to — it's quite harsh, and it sounds like it's been with you for a while, possibly long before this long-distance situation ever began. Compassion isn't letting yourself off a hook; it's actually what gives us the steadiness to keep showing up, which you've already been doing even without it. 

I'm wondering — do you have any sense of where that voice learned that softness toward yourself is something you have to earn rather than something you simply deserve?

client: That's... a hard question to sit with. I think part of me wants to say it came from my parents, the way they'd only really acknowledge me when I did something right, but saying that out loud feels like I'm just making excuses or blaming them. And honestly, I'm not even sure I deserve softness right now, because if I'd just been more attentive to the relationship, maybe things with my partner wouldn't feel so strained across the distance.
therapist:
Naming where that voice came from isn't making excuses — it's actually doing the brave, honest work of understanding yourself, and those two things are very different. I also want to gently point out that you just connected the distance feeling "strained" to something being wrong with *you*, when strain across distance is simply what distance does; it doesn't require a personal failing to explain it. 

I'm curious — what would it mean for you if the strain in the relationship turned out to be nobody's fault, just an genuinely hard situation that two people are navigating together?

client: That's... a strange thought to sit with, honestly. Like, part of me wants to believe it, but there's this other part that keeps saying if it were really nobody's fault, then why do I feel so guilty all the time? I guess I'm not sure I'd even know how to stop looking for what I did wrong.
therapist:
The guilt feels like evidence of wrongdoing, but it's worth considering that guilt can also be what happens when a caring person desperately wants *some* control over a painful situation — if it's your fault, then maybe you could fix it, and that's less terrifying than accepting that you can't fully control love across distance. That instinct to search for what you did wrong might actually be a form of self-protection, not a sign that you truly are to blame. 

What do you think it might feel like to sit with the uncertainty of "this is just hard" rather than the familiar weight of "this is my fault to solve"?

client: Honestly, that reframe kind of stopped me for a second, because I never thought about the guilt as something I was doing to feel more in control. But sitting with "this is just hard" feels almost worse, because at least if it's my fault, I have something to work on, some action I can take to maybe fix things with my friend across the country. If I let go of the blame, I'm just left with this helpless feeling that the distance might slowly swallow the friendship and there's nothing I can do about it.
therapist:
You've just uncovered something really important — that the blame, as painful as it is, has been quietly protecting you from feeling helpless, and helplessness can feel even more unbearable than guilt because it leaves your hands empty. But I want to reflect back that your hands aren't actually empty here; you've been showing up to calls, to a course, to this conversation, and those are all real choices you're making *toward* connection rather than passively waiting for distance to win. 

I'm wondering — when you think about the relationship with your partner specifically, are there small, concrete things that might help you feel like an active participant in nurturing it, rather than someone just hoping the distance doesn't take over?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that those things count for something. But honestly, when I think about doing something "concrete" with my partner, I just freeze up — like, what if I try and it still doesn't feel close, you know? That almost feels worse than not trying, because then I can't even blame the distance anymore.
therapist:
What you're describing is a really understandable protective move — if you don't try, the distance stays the "villain" and you stay safe from the scarier possibility that trying might not be enough. But I want to gently name that this fear of trying is actually keeping you more frozen than the distance itself is, and that's something you do have some agency over, even if it feels small. 

What might it look like to try something very low-stakes — not to "fix" the closeness, but just as a small experiment where there's no way to really fail?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows you're probably right that I'm protecting myself. But when you say "no way to really fail," I'm not sure I believe that — like, what if I reach out to my brother and he responds with that same flat, one-word reply he always gives, or just doesn't respond at all? That still feels like failing, even if you'd call it data or an experiment or whatever.
therapist:
Your instinct to push back on that is actually really healthy, and you're right — a flat reply would genuinely sting, and I don't want to minimize that by wrapping it in clinical language. What I'm more curious about is that you shifted from your partner to your brother just now, which makes me wonder if there's something important there about where you're most afraid of not being enough. 

Can you tell me a little more about what's happening with your brother, and what that relationship has been feeling like for you lately?
